questions.title: A substance cleared faster than inulin but slower than PAH is filtered and partially secreted
questions.question: A substance's renal clearance is measured as higher than inulin clearance but lower than PAH (para-aminohippurate) clearance. What is the renal handling of this substance?
questions.subject: renal

options.A: It is freely filtered and partially secreted by the renal tubules
options.B: It is freely filtered and completely reabsorbed, with no secretion
options.C: It is freely filtered and neither reabsorbed nor secreted, exactly like inulin
options.D: It is freely filtered and completely secreted, exactly like PAH

explanations.A: Correct. Inulin clearance equals GFR (freely filtered, neither reabsorbed nor secreted), while PAH clearance approximates renal plasma flow (freely filtered and virtually completely secreted). A clearance value between these two therefore indicates a substance that is freely filtered and also partially secreted by the tubules, adding to its filtered load without reaching the near-complete secretion seen with PAH.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Net reabsorption would give a clearance LOWER than inulin (GFR), not a value between inulin and PAH clearance.
explanations.C: Incorrect. A clearance equal to inulin's would indicate no net reabsorption or secretion; a clearance higher than inulin's rules this out.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Complete secretion, like PAH, would give a clearance approximately equal to PAH clearance itself, not a value below it.

questions.learning_objective: State that a substance whose renal clearance lies between inulin clearance (=GFR) and PAH clearance (≈renal plasma flow) is freely filtered and partially secreted by the renal tubules.

questions.title: Basolateral Na+/K+-ATPase drives sodium reabsorption across the proximal convoluted tubule
questions.question: Sodium reabsorption across the proximal convoluted tubule epithelium is ultimately driven by which mechanism?
questions.subject: renal

options.A: The basolateral Na+/K+-ATPase pump, which maintains the low intracellular sodium gradient that drives apical sodium entry
options.B: Passive diffusion down a favorable electrochemical gradient alone, without any active transport step
options.C: The H+/K+-ATPase pump located in intercalated cells of the collecting duct
options.D: Aldosterone-dependent epithelial sodium channels (ENaC), as in the principal cells of the collecting duct

explanations.A: Correct. The basolateral Na+/K+-ATPase actively pumps sodium out of the proximal tubule cell into the interstitium (in exchange for potassium), keeping intracellular sodium low. This gradient is what drives sodium's passive entry across the apical membrane via numerous cotransporters and exchangers (with glucose, amino acids, phosphate, and via Na+/H+ exchange), making the basolateral pump the ultimate energetic driver of proximal sodium reabsorption.
explanations.B: Incorrect. While apical entry into the cell is passive (facilitated by the gradient the pump creates), overall net reabsorption is an active transport process fundamentally dependent on the ATP-consuming basolateral pump, not passive diffusion alone.
explanations.C: Incorrect. H+/K+-ATPase in intercalated cells mediates potassium reabsorption and hydrogen secretion in the distal nephron/collecting duct, not proximal tubular sodium reabsorption.
explanations.D: Incorrect. ENaC channels mediate aldosterone-regulated sodium reabsorption in the principal cells of the distal tubule and collecting duct, a distinct, more distal and hormonally regulated mechanism from the constitutive Na+/K+-ATPase-driven reabsorption of the proximal tubule.

questions.learning_objective: State that sodium reabsorption across the proximal convoluted tubule is ultimately driven by the basolateral Na+/K+-ATPase pump, which maintains the low intracellular sodium gradient enabling apical sodium entry.

questions.title: Angiotensin II stimulates proximal tubular sodium-hydrogen exchange, increasing sodium and bicarbonate reabsorption
questions.question: Which of the following is a true statement regarding the direct renal tubular actions of angiotensin II?
questions.subject: renal

options.A: Angiotensin II stimulates proximal tubular Na+/H+ exchange, increasing sodium and bicarbonate reabsorption
options.B: Angiotensin II inhibits proximal tubular sodium reabsorption, promoting natriuresis
options.C: Angiotensin II acts only on the renal vasculature (efferent arteriole) and has no direct tubular effect
options.D: Angiotensin II decreases bicarbonate reabsorption, favoring the development of metabolic acidosis

explanations.A: Correct. In addition to its vascular and aldosterone-mediated effects, angiotensin II directly stimulates the apical Na+/H+ exchanger (NHE3) in the proximal tubule. This increases sodium reabsorption (paired with hydrogen secretion) and, because the secreted hydrogen ion combines with filtered bicarbonate to regenerate CO2 that re-enters the cell and is converted back to reabsorbed bicarbonate, also increases net bicarbonate reabsorption — part of the overall volume- and pressure-conserving action of the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Angiotensin II promotes, rather than inhibits, proximal sodium reabsorption; it is an antinatriuretic hormone that supports volume conservation, opposite to what this option describes.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Beyond its vascular actions, angiotensin II has well-established direct tubular effects, especially at the proximal tubule (Na+/H+ exchange) in addition to its aldosterone-mediated distal effects; it is not confined to vascular action alone.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Angiotensin II increases, rather than decreases, bicarbonate reabsorption via enhanced proximal Na+/H+ exchange, and its overall hemodynamic/volume effects do not characteristically favor metabolic acidosis.

questions.learning_objective: State that angiotensin II directly stimulates proximal tubular Na+/H+ exchange, increasing both sodium and bicarbonate reabsorption.

questions.title: The left kidney is separated anteriorly from the stomach by the omental bursa (lesser sac)
questions.question: The left kidney is related anteriorly to the stomach, being separated from it by which peritoneal space?
questions.subject: renal

options.B: The greater sac (general peritoneal cavity) directly

explanations.A: Correct. The posterior wall of the stomach and the anterior surface of the left kidney (upper pole) are both related through the omental bursa (lesser sac). This is the peritoneal space that lies posterior to the stomach and lesser omentum, also bordered by the pancreas and spleen. The stomach is therefore an indirect (bursa-separated) anterior relation of the left kidney rather than one in direct peritoneal contact.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The greater sac is the main peritoneal cavity anterior to the lesser sac; the stomach's posterior surface, which relates to the left kidney, faces into the lesser sac (omental bursa), not directly into the greater sac.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The hepatorenal recess (Morison's pouch) lies on the right side, between the liver and right kidney, and is unrelated to the left kidney's relation to the stomach.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The rectouterine pouch (pouch of Douglas) is a pelvic peritoneal recess between the uterus and rectum, unrelated to the upper abdominal relation between the left kidney and stomach.

questions.learning_objective: State that the stomach relates anteriorly to the left kidney through the omental bursa (lesser sac), the peritoneal space posterior to the stomach.

questions.title: Gartner's duct cysts are vestigial remnants of the mesonephric (Wolffian) duct
questions.question: Gartner's duct cysts, found along the anterolateral wall of the vagina, are vestigial remnants of which embryonic structure?
questions.subject: gyn

options.D: The mesonephric tubules (as opposed to the duct itself)

explanations.A: Correct. In the female, the mesonephric (Wolffian) duct normally regresses, since it is not stabilized by testosterone the way it is in the male. Residual segments can nonetheless persist along the lateral wall of the uterus, cervix, or vagina. When the vaginal-level remnant persists and dilates, it forms a Gartner's duct cyst, a classic incidental finding on pelvic examination.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The paramesonephric (Müllerian) duct is the structure that persists and develops in the female (forming the uterine tubes, uterus, cervix and upper vagina); Gartner's duct is instead the vestige of the duct that regresses in females (the mesonephric duct), not the one that develops.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The urogenital sinus contributes to the lower vagina and vestibule, but Gartner's duct cysts specifically represent a mesonephric duct remnant, not a urogenital sinus derivative.
explanations.D: Incorrect. It is the mesonephric duct itself (the longitudinal collecting structure), not the individual mesonephric tubules, that forms the residual, persisting Gartner's duct along the vaginal wall.

questions.learning_objective: State that gartner's duct cysts are vestigial remnants of the mesonephric (Wolffian) duct, which normally regresses in the female but can leave a persistent, occasionally cystic, remnant along the lateral vaginal wall.

questions.title: A duplicated (double) ureter draining a single kidney results from early splitting of the ureteric bud
questions.question: A duplicated (double) ureter draining a single kidney most commonly results from which embryological event?
questions.subject: renal

options.A: Early (premature) splitting of the ureteric bud, before it reaches the metanephric blastema
options.B: Persistence of two entirely separate metanephric blastemas within one kidney
options.C: Failure of the mesonephric duct to degenerate after the ureteric bud arises
options.D: Late splitting of the ureteric bud, after it has already entered the metanephric blastema

explanations.A: Correct. A complete duplex (double) ureter, each with its own separate ureteric orifice, results when the ureteric bud splits early, before it induces the metanephric blastema. Two entirely separate ureteric bud stalks then each induce their own collecting system within a single, fused kidney. This is termed complete ureteral duplication.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The metanephric blastema (metanephric mesenchyme) is a single mass of intermediate mesoderm that is induced by the ureteric bud; duplication anomalies arise from abnormal branching of the ureteric bud itself, not from two separate blastemas.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Persistence of mesonephric duct remnants (e.g., Gartner's duct in females, appendix epididymis in males) is a separate embryological event unrelated to ureteric duplication, which concerns abnormal branching of the ureteric bud.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Splitting of the ureteric bud AFTER it has already entered and begun inducing the metanephric blastema produces a partial (incomplete/bifid) duplication — two ureters that join before reaching the bladder — rather than the complete duplication with two separate ureteric orifices that results from early splitting.

questions.learning_objective: State that complete duplication of the ureter draining a single kidney results from early splitting of the ureteric bud, before it reaches and induces the metanephric blastema.

questions.title: Linear IgG/C3 immunofluorescence with crescent formation defines Goodpasture syndrome (anti-GBM disease)
questions.question: Renal biopsy in a patient with a pulmonary-renal syndrome shows linear immunofluorescent staining for IgG and C3 along the glomerular basement membrane, together with proliferation of parietal epithelial cells forming crescents. Which diagnosis is most consistent with these findings?
questions.subject: renal

explanations.A: Correct. Goodpasture syndrome (anti-GBM disease) is caused by autoantibodies directed against an epitope on type IV collagen shared by the glomerular and alveolar basement membranes. On immunofluorescence this produces a smooth, continuous linear pattern of IgG (and often C3) deposition along the GBM — distinct from the granular ('lumpy-bumpy') pattern of immune-complex diseases — and the resulting severe glomerular injury classically triggers proliferation of parietal (Bowman's capsule) epithelial cells into crescents, producing rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis with concurrent pulmonary hemorrhage.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis is an immune-complex disease showing a granular ('lumpy-bumpy'), not linear, pattern of IgG/C3 deposition, reflecting discrete subepithelial immune complex deposits rather than antibody binding diffusely along the GBM.
explanations.C: Incorrect. IgA nephropathy shows mesangial, not linear GBM, immunofluorescence positivity — IgA deposits are localized to the mesangium rather than diffusely along the capillary basement membrane.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Membranous nephropathy shows a granular, subepithelial ('spike-and-dome') pattern of immune complex deposition, not a linear pattern, and does not characteristically produce crescents.

questions.learning_objective: State that linear immunofluorescent IgG/C3 deposition along the glomerular basement membrane, with parietal epithelial cell proliferation forming crescents, defines anti-GBM disease (Goodpasture syndrome).

questions.title: Idiopathic membranous glomerulonephritis is not a feature of diabetic glomerulosclerosis
questions.question: All of the following are characteristic features of diabetic glomerulosclerosis EXCEPT:
questions.subject: renal

options.A: Idiopathic membranous glomerulonephritis with subepithelial spike-and-dome deposits
options.C: Diffuse thickening of the glomerular basement membrane
options.D: Hyalinization of both the afferent and efferent arterioles

explanations.A: Correct. Idiopathic membranous glomerulonephritis is a distinct, separate glomerular disease, typically caused by autoantibodies such as anti-PLA2R producing subepithelial 'spike-and-dome' immune deposits. It is not a feature or component of diabetic glomerulosclerosis. Diabetic glomerulosclerosis instead has its own characteristic set of glomerular and vascular changes, described in the other three options.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Kimmelstiel-Wilson nodular glomerulosclerosis — eosinophilic, PAS-positive nodules within the glomerular mesangium — IS a hallmark, relatively specific histologic feature of diabetic nephropathy, so it does not answer this 'except' question.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Diffuse thickening of the glomerular basement membrane (from non-enzymatic glycosylation and increased matrix protein deposition) IS an early and characteristic feature of diabetic glomerulosclerosis, so it does not answer this 'except' question.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Hyaline arteriolosclerosis affecting BOTH the afferent and efferent arterioles is a distinctive feature of diabetic nephropathy (unlike hypertensive nephrosclerosis, which characteristically spares the efferent arteriole), so it does not answer this 'except' question.

questions.learning_objective: State that diabetic glomerulosclerosis is characterized by diffuse GBM thickening, Kimmelstiel-Wilson nodular glomerulosclerosis, and hyalinization of both afferent and efferent arterioles — but not by idiopathic membranous glomerulonephritis, which is a separate disease entity.

questions.title: Severe hypercalcemia with concurrent heart failure is initially treated with isotonic saline followed by a loop diuretic
questions.question: A patient with severe hypercalcemia and concomitant heart failure requires urgent lowering of serum calcium. Which initial treatment approach is most appropriate?
questions.subject: renal

options.A: Isotonic (normal) saline to restore intravascular volume, followed by a loop diuretic to promote calciuresis, with careful monitoring given the heart failure
options.B: Thiazide diuretics, which enhance distal tubular calcium reabsorption
options.C: Aggressive free-water restriction alone, without intravenous fluids or diuretics
options.D: Immediate administration of high-dose calcium channel blockers

explanations.A: Correct. Severe hypercalcemia is usually accompanied by volume depletion (from calcium-induced nephrogenic diabetes insipidus and reduced oral intake), so initial management is isotonic saline to restore volume and increase renal calcium excretion by improving GFR and reducing proximal tubular sodium (and paired calcium) reabsorption. A loop diuretic (e.g., furosemide) is then added, both to further promote calciuresis by blocking calcium reabsorption in the thick ascending limb and to prevent fluid overload — a particularly important consideration in a patient who also has heart failure and cannot tolerate large-volume saline without careful monitoring.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Thiazide diuretics increase distal tubular calcium reabsorption and would worsen, not improve, hypercalcemia; they are contraindicated in this setting (and are instead used therapeutically to reduce urinary calcium excretion in conditions like idiopathic hypercalciuria).
explanations.C: Incorrect. Hypercalcemic patients are typically volume-depleted, and free-water restriction without volume repletion would fail to correct the underlying deficit and would not promote the renal calcium excretion needed to lower serum calcium.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Calcium channel blockers are not a standard treatment for hypercalcemia; the priority is volume repletion and calciuresis (saline plus loop diuretic), with agents such as bisphosphonates or calcitonin considered for more definitive/sustained lowering afterward.

questions.learning_objective: State that severe hypercalcemia is initially managed with isotonic saline to restore volume, followed by a loop diuretic to promote calciuresis, with careful attention to fluid balance when heart failure coexists.

questions.title: Uroplakins allow bladder umbrella cells to increase luminal surface area while stretching without losing barrier integrity
questions.question: Uroplakins, specialized transmembrane proteins in the apical plasma membrane of umbrella (superficial) cells of the urinary bladder, primarily function to:
questions.subject: renal

options.A: Form rigid membrane plaques that let the urothelium increase its luminal surface area and stretch as the bladder fills, while maintaining an impermeable barrier
options.B: Actively transport sodium and water across the urothelium into the underlying lamina propria
options.C: Secrete a protective mucus layer over the underlying lamina propria
options.D: Generate rhythmic peristaltic contractions of the bladder wall

explanations.A: Correct. Uroplakins assemble into rigid, plaque-like structures within the apical membrane of umbrella cells, separated by more flexible hinge regions. As the bladder fills, these plaques can unfold and slide relative to one another (and the umbrella cells themselves flatten), allowing the urothelial surface area to increase substantially to accommodate distension, while the plaques' tight molecular packing keeps the epithelium a highly impermeable barrier that prevents urine solutes from diffusing across into the underlying tissue.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The urothelium, especially at the umbrella cell layer, is characterized by very LOW permeability and minimal active transport, precisely because uroplakins create a barrier rather than a transport surface — this impermeability is essential to prevent osmotic gradients from disrupting the underlying tissue.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Mucus secretion is not a recognized function of uroplakins or the urothelial umbrella cell layer generally; barrier function here depends on the plaque structure itself, not a secreted mucus coat.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Peristaltic/contractile activity of the bladder wall is a function of the detrusor smooth muscle, not the uroplakin-containing apical membrane of the surface urothelial cells.

questions.learning_objective: State that uroplakins form rigid apical membrane plaques in bladder umbrella cells that allow the urothelium to increase surface area and stretch during bladder filling while maintaining a highly impermeable barrier.

questions.title: During prolonged fasting the renal cortex contributes significantly to glucose production via gluconeogenesis
questions.question: During prolonged fasting, the kidney (specifically the renal cortex) becomes an important site of energy/glucose production through which metabolic pathway?
questions.subject: fnd

options.A: Gluconeogenesis, using substrates such as glutamine and lactate, contributing significantly to glucose production alongside the liver
options.B: Anaerobic glycolysis exclusively, producing lactate as its end product for export
options.C: Ketogenesis, exporting ketone bodies for use by peripheral tissues
options.D: Glycogenolysis, drawing on substantial renal glycogen reserves

explanations.A: Correct. During prolonged fasting/starvation, the renal cortex becomes a significant gluconeogenic organ, using substrates such as glutamine (also linked to renal ammoniagenesis for acid-base regulation), lactate, glycerol and amino acids to synthesize glucose. As starvation progresses, the kidney can contribute a substantial fraction (up to roughly 40–50% in prolonged fasting) of total endogenous glucose production, complementing hepatic gluconeogenesis.
explanations.B: Incorrect. While the renal medulla is characteristically dependent on anaerobic glycolysis (due to its low oxygen tension), the renal CORTEX — the site relevant to fasting energy production discussed here — is instead a major site of gluconeogenesis, not glycolysis, and is a net glucose producer rather than consumer during fasting.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Ketogenesis (synthesis of ketone bodies from fatty acid-derived acetyl-CoA) occurs in the liver, not the kidney; the kidney can utilize ketone bodies as fuel but is not a site of their synthesis.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The kidney has minimal glycogen stores compared with the liver and skeletal muscle, and glycogenolysis is not a meaningful contributor to renal glucose output during fasting — the kidney's contribution instead comes from de novo gluconeogenesis.

questions.learning_objective: State that during prolonged fasting, the renal cortex becomes a significant site of gluconeogenesis, using substrates such as glutamine and lactate to contribute meaningfully to whole-body glucose production alongside the liver.

questions.title: Roughly 98% of total body L-carnitine is stored in skeletal and cardiac muscle
questions.question: Which of the following best describes the tissue distribution of L-carnitine in the body?
questions.subject: fnd

options.A: Approximately 98% of total body carnitine is stored within skeletal and cardiac muscle, where it is required for fatty acid beta-oxidation
options.B: Carnitine is stored predominantly within adipose tissue, packaged together with stored triglyceride
options.C: Carnitine is confined almost entirely to the liver, its sole site of utilization
options.D: Carnitine circulates freely in plasma and is not appreciably stored within any body tissue

explanations.A: Correct. Skeletal and cardiac muscle, which rely heavily on fatty acid beta-oxidation for ATP production (especially cardiac muscle at rest and skeletal muscle during sustained/endurance activity), together account for roughly 98% of total body carnitine stores. Carnitine is essential in these tissues for shuttling long-chain fatty acyl groups across the inner mitochondrial membrane via the carnitine shuttle (CPT-I/CPT-II), a rate-limiting step for beta-oxidation.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Although adipose tissue is the storage site for triglyceride (the fatty acid reservoir carnitine helps mobilize for oxidation elsewhere), carnitine itself is not predominantly stored in adipose tissue but in muscle, where the oxidative machinery it supports is concentrated.
explanations.C: Incorrect. While the liver synthesizes carnitine (from lysine and methionine) and also uses it for hepatic fatty acid oxidation, the great majority of the body's total carnitine pool resides in skeletal and cardiac muscle, not the liver.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The vast majority of body carnitine is intracellular, concentrated within muscle tissue, with only a small fraction circulating in plasma at any time.

questions.learning_objective: State that approximately 98% of total body L-carnitine is stored within skeletal and cardiac muscle, tissues that depend heavily on fatty acid beta-oxidation for energy.

questions.title: Streptococcus pyogenes is the classic cause of non-suppurative post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis
questions.question: A patient develops acute glomerulonephritis, a non-suppurative complication, two to three weeks after a preceding infection. Which organism is the classic causative agent?
questions.subject: inf

options.A: Streptococcus pyogenes (group A beta-hemolytic streptococcus), specifically nephritogenic strains

explanations.A: Correct. Post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis is a non-suppurative immune-complex complication of infection (classically pharyngitis or impetigo) with specific 'nephritogenic' strains of Streptococcus pyogenes (group A beta-hemolytic streptococcus). Streptococcal antigens (e.g., streptococcal pyrogenic exotoxin B/nephritis-associated plasmin receptor) trigger immune complex formation and deposition along the glomerular basement membrane, producing the characteristic latent period of roughly 2–3 weeks (pharyngitis) or 3–6 weeks (skin infection) before nephritic symptoms appear.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Staphylococcus aureus is more classically associated with a distinct entity, IgA-dominant post-infectious (staphylococcal) glomerulonephritis, typically in a different clinical setting (e.g., associated with ongoing/active infection such as endocarditis or a deep abscess, rather than the classic 2-3 week latent-period nephritic syndrome after pharyngitis).
explanations.C: Incorrect. Streptococcus pneumoniae is not the classic causative organism of post-infectious glomerulonephritis; that role belongs specifically to group A Streptococcus pyogenes.
explanations.D: Incorrect. E. coli is the leading cause of urinary tract infection, not of the non-suppurative, immune-complex-mediated glomerulonephritis being described here.

questions.learning_objective: State that streptococcus pyogenes (specifically nephritogenic strains of group A beta-hemolytic streptococcus) is the classic causative organism of non-suppurative post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis.
